extracted.intended_audience: judges, litigators, corporate counsel, discovery counsel, and data controllers handling cross-border e-discovery and data protection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and model orders for preserving, producing, and protecting Protected Data in U.S. litigation that implicates foreign Data Protection Laws, including model pretrial and protective order language and principles for reasonable records management, data minimization, and cross-border discovery procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records management discipline / avoid indiscriminate retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Records and information do not need to be preserved when they are no longer needed for business or legal reasons; organizations should avoid electronic data hoarding and apply records management lifecycle discipline to ESI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce the amount of data created and retained before preservation and discovery obligations attach; recognize direct and indirect costs and security risks of unbridled accumulation; take good faith, reasonable efforts to retain, manage, and dispose of inactive data both prospectively and retrospectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation obligation tied to notice of litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A litigant’s duty to preserve relevant information arises once the litigant is on notice of actual or reasonably anticipated litigation and need not keep all information forever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable and systematic records management rules can be applied provided they are applied uniformly and not in a fashion to avoid a litigant’s common law duty to preserve relevant information once on notice of litigation (citing Arthur Andersen LLP v. United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit preservation duration to pending or reasonably anticipated litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The preservation obligation is limited in duration to the time that a legal action is pending or remains reasonably anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable anticipation of litigation arises when an organization is on notice of a credible probability that it will become involved in litigation, seriously contemplates initiating litigation, or takes specific actions to commence litigation; preservation conduct is judged on facts and circumstances and frequently assessed after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data minimization / privacy by design
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement privacy by design as part of data minimization so that data processing is 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary' for processing purposes (GDPR art.5(1)(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed privacy and data protection throughout the lifecycle of technologies, from design to deployment and disposal; taking into account state of the art, cost, nature/scope/context/purposes of processing and risks, implement technical and organisational measures (e.g., pseudonymisation) to meet GDPR requirements and protect data subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect integrity, reliability, access, confidentiality, and security while preserving data
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to preserve Protected Data is accompanied by a corresponding obligation to take reasonable steps to protect the reliability, integrity, access, confidentiality, and security of the data while it is being preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement meaningful privacy-by-design protections in new ESI systems; continue to observe substantive data protection and confidentiality requirements even when distributing notice of and requiring compliance with legal hold notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit preservation/discovery to relevant and necessary information (proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation or discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting scope minimizes conflicts of law and impacts on data subjects; courts and parties should employ proportionality to minimize conflicts with Data Protection Laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith and reasonableness standard where conflicts exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Where full compliance with both Data Protection Laws and preservation/disclosure/discovery obligations presents a conflict, a party’s conduct should be judged by a court or data protection authority under a standard of good faith and reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is intended to provide assurance to non-U.S. data protection officials and to guide assessment of conduct where legal obligations conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stipulation or court order to minimize conflicts with Data Protection Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a conflict exists between Data Protection Laws and preservation, disclosure, or discovery obligations, a stipulation or court order should be employed to protect Protected Data and minimize the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should seek protective mechanisms (stipulations/orders) to reconcile obligations and protect data subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data controllers must be prepared to demonstrate safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: A Data Controller subject to preservation, disclosure, or discovery obligations should be prepared to demonstrate that data protection obligations have been addressed and that appropriate data protection safeguards have been instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to show courts or authorities the measures taken to protect Protected Data when complying with discovery obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit retention of Protected Data to legal or business necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Data Controllers should retain Protected Data only as long as necessary to satisfy legal or business needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While litigation is pending or reasonably anticipated, preserve relevant information including Protected Data with appropriate data safeguards; otherwise dispose of inactive data consistent with records management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties must disclose intent to initiate foreign discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Within specified days, any party intending to initiate discovery outside the United States shall file and serve a statement disclosing its intention, including whether Hague Convention, Letters Rogatory, foreign deponents, documents located outside the U.S., and awareness of blocking statutes or Data Protection Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure should identify applicable laws and the countries involved, and provide as much information as possible about potential foreign legal constraints on discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding parties must state opposition and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Other parties shall respond to the initial disclosure by stating to what extent they will or will not oppose such foreign discovery and, if opposing, concisely state the nature of the opposition and the reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This promotes narrowing disputes and early identification of contested issues regarding international discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer on international discovery scope and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties shall meet and confer to discuss reaching agreement or narrowing disputes concerning conducting discovery outside the United States, completion dates, objections, and protective orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include topics such as methods of conducting discovery, scheduling international discovery completion, timing of objections to the court, and protective order contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court scheduling and motion deadlines for international discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may set deadlines for initiation/completion of international discovery and require motions on international discovery issues to be filed by specified dates with expedited response and reply schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model language sets responses due within 14 days and replies within 14 days after response to permit prompt adjudication of international discovery disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of foreign officials/contact information when relying on blocking statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: A party relying on blocking statutes or data protection rules must state its knowledge of the practice as applied to the case, its position on the issue, and provide contact information for the foreign official or judge knowledgeable or authorized to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables the court to assess and, if appropriate, communicate with foreign authorities regarding authorization or facilitation of discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court engagement with foreign authorities if normal means fail
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain discovery is relevant but cannot be secured by normal means under the Federal Rules, conventions, or other recognized procedures, the court may itself initiate communications with a foreign data protection official or court to determine if discovery can be authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This empowers courts to facilitate cross-border discovery where procedural or legal barriers exist abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage adoption of Sedona international discovery principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The court encourages parties to adopt Sedona Conference Principles: respect foreign Data Protection Laws; judge conflicts by good faith/reasonableness; limit preservation/discovery to relevant/necessary data; use stipulations/orders to protect data; Data Controllers demonstrate safeguards; retain Protected Data only as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles summarize the document's core recommendations for reconciling discovery and data protection obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Protective Order to discovery material
rubrics_metrics.description: A Protective Order governs handling of documents, depositions, deposition exhibits, interrogatory responses, responses to requests for admissions, responses to requests for production, and all other discovery obtained pursuant to the Federal Rules (collectively 'Discovery Material').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define Producing/Receiving Party and Authorized Recipient, and specify that the Order applies to discovery material except where limited by other paragraphs of the order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation standards for Confidential and Highly Confidential material
rubrics_metrics.description: Any Producing Party may designate Discovery Material as 'Confidential' or 'Highly Confidential' if it in good faith reasonably believes the material contains non-public, confidential, or highly sensitive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and care in making designations; mass, indiscriminate, or routinized designations are prohibited; designations should be limited to specific qualifying material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Confidential Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential Material includes any information believed in good faith to be confidential or sensitive, including trade secrets, research, design, development, financial, technical, marketing, planning, personal, or commercial information (per Rule 26(c)(1)(G)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Rule 26(c)(1)(G) and applicable case law to guide what qualifies as Confidential Material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Highly Confidential Material and Protected Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly Confidential Material includes Protected Data and/or Confidential Material that contains extremely sensitive, non-public information (e.g., non-public product design/testing, trade secrets) whose disclosure would create substantial risk of competitive or business injury. Protected Data refers to information believed to be subject to federal, state, or foreign Data Protection Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain Protected Data may require alternative or additional protections; parties should meet and confer or move the court for appropriate relief. Protected Data examples include financial, medical, EU personal data (GDPR), UK Data Protection Act, PIPEDA, APPI, etc.; list must be updated/tailored per jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertent disclosure remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: The inadvertent failure to designate Discovery Material as Confidential or Highly Confidential does not constitute a waiver of such claim and may be remedied by prompt supplemental written notice upon discovery of the inadvertent disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once notice is given, the material will be subject to the protections of the Order; Receiving Parties must take steps to restrict access and re-mark copies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of copies and derivatives of protected material
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of Discovery Material become Confidential or Highly Confidential to the same extent as the original; notes, lists, memoranda, indices, and compilations that quote from, paraphrase, copy, or disclose Confidential/Highly Confidential Material with sufficient specificity shall be accorded the same status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving Parties must mark copies with appropriate legends and limit availability to authorized persons; exercise good faith to ensure copies and downstream disseminations are treated consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for designating documents, depositions, non-written materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Protective Order requires specific procedures for designating Documents, Deposition and Other Proceedings, and Non-Written Materials as Confidential or Highly Confidential (placeholders in the model indicate where parties/court should insert details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should specify marking procedures for each category (e.g., stamping documents, stating on the record at depositions, labeling non-written materials) and include timelines and methods for retroactive designation if needed.
